title: THEY ATTACKED ME BEFORE THEY EVEN READ WHAT I WROTE… BUT THE MOST PAINFUL PART WAS WHAT IT REVEALED ABOUT OUR HEARTS
paragraphs: THEY ATTACKED ME BEFORE THEY EVEN READ WHAT I WROTE… BUT THE MOST PAINFUL PART WAS WHAT IT REVEALED ABOUT OUR HEARTS

When Christians become quicker to accuse than to understand, something is terribly wrong. And what Jesus endured at the hands of those who judged Him should make every one of us examine how we treat others.
Some people have already decided I'm wrong before they even finish reading what I wrote.
They see a title.
They read a sentence.
They notice a word that makes them uncomfortable.
And suddenly, the accusations begin.
Not questions.
Not a sincere attempt to understand.
Accusations.
Sometimes harsh. Sometimes personal. Sometimes wrapped in Bible verses, as though quoting Scripture automatically makes every judgment righteous.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part is that some of these accusations come from people who openly profess to follow Jesus Christ.
I have sat with that reality.
Not because I believe I am above correction. I am not.
Not because everything I write is perfect. It isn't.
And certainly not because I expect everyone to agree with me.
But because I keep wondering something that should trouble every believer who loves the truth.
When did we become so eager to condemn someone that we no longer feel responsible for understanding what they actually said?
And before anyone assumes this article is simply my attempt to defend myself, please stay with me.
Because what I am about to share may challenge me just as much as it challenges those who criticize me.
This is not merely about people attacking an article.
It is about something much deeper.
Something Scripture warned us about long before social media existed.
And somewhere between the accusations, the wounded pride, the temptation to retaliate, and the uncomfortable truth of God's Word, I found myself facing a question I could not escape.
Am I more concerned about defending my reputation, or reflecting the character of Jesus Christ?
That question changed the direction of this entire conversation.
Because the moment we open Scripture, we discover that the problem is not new.
The platforms have changed.
The speed of judgment has changed.
But the human heart?
The human heart still desperately needs redemption.
In James 1:19, Scripture gives us an instruction that almost feels revolutionary in a world addicted to instant reactions.
ἔστω δὲ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ταχὺς εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι, βραδὺς εἰς τὸ λαλῆσαι, βραδὺς εἰς ὀργήν.
The Greek teaches that every person should be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.
Notice the order.
Hearing comes before speaking.
Understanding comes before reacting.
Patience comes before anger.
James does not say we should be quick to form an opinion and then search for evidence to defend it.
He does not tell us to react first and investigate later.
He calls believers to a posture of humility that allows truth to be heard before conclusions are formed.
And that should make us uncomfortable.
Because how often do we do exactly the opposite?
We see a headline and immediately assume we know the entire argument.
We encounter a sentence that challenges our understanding and decide the author must be dangerous.
We hear something unfamiliar and mistake our discomfort for spiritual discernment.
Then we respond publicly, sometimes before asking even one sincere question.
But being offended by something does not automatically mean that something is false.
And being confident in our interpretation does not automatically mean we have understood another person's meaning.
Discernment requires truth. Accusation requires only suspicion.
Those are not the same thing.
Proverbs 18:13 says:
"He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him." — KJV
The Hebrew is equally piercing:
מֵשִׁיב דָּבָר בְּטֶרֶם יִשְׁמָע אִוֶּלֶת הִיא־לוֹ וּכְלִמָּה
The opening words, mēshîb dābār beterem yishmāʿ, describe answering a matter before hearing it.
The proverb identifies such conduct as foolishness and disgrace.
Not courage.
Not boldness.
Not spiritual maturity.
Foolishness.
That is a sobering word.
Especially when we remember how easily Christians can mistake the intensity of their reaction for the righteousness of their position.
You can be passionate and still be mistaken.
You can quote Scripture and still misapply it.
You can defend a true doctrine while behaving in a way that contradicts the character of the Savior you claim to represent.
And yes, you can also write an article with sincere intentions and still communicate something poorly.
I know that possibility applies to me.
That is why I welcome sincere questions, thoughtful disagreement, and biblical correction.
If I have misrepresented Scripture, show me where.
If I have misunderstood a passage, help me examine it.
If my wording creates confusion, give me the opportunity to clarify it.
I would rather be corrected by God's Word than protected by my own pride.
But there is a difference between correcting an error and attacking a person without first understanding the message.
And that difference matters deeply to God.
John 7:24 records Jesus saying:
"Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment." — KJV
The original Greek reads:
μὴ κρίνετε κατ᾽ ὄψιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν κρίνατε.
The expression dikaian krisin refers to righteous judgment.
Jesus was not forbidding all moral evaluation.
He was confronting superficial judgment.
Judgment based merely on outward appearance rather than what is actually right.
The immediate context concerns people who were judging Jesus' actions concerning the Sabbath without rightly understanding the matter.
That context is important.
We must not turn this verse into a convenient weapon against everyone who disagrees with us.
Righteous judgment is necessary.
The church must test teachings against Scripture.
False teaching must be challenged.
Sin must not be excused simply because correction makes someone uncomfortable.
But righteous judgment must actually be righteous.
It must be informed.
It must be fair.
It must submit to the truth rather than manipulate the truth to justify a reaction.
And this is where I want to speak directly to those who have criticized my writing.
You are welcome to disagree with me. But please understand what I am saying before deciding what I believe.
Read the context.
Consider the Scripture.
Examine the reasoning.
Ask questions.
And if something is wrong, correct it with biblical evidence.
I am not asking for unquestioning agreement.
I am asking for the kind of fairness we would all want extended to ourselves.
Because one day, you may be the person whose words are misunderstood.
One day, someone may take a sentence you wrote in sincerity and use it to construct a version of you that does not exist.
One day, you may find yourself trying to explain something that people have already decided not to hear.
And in that moment, you will understand how painful it is to be judged by an accusation rather than by the truth.
But here is where this story becomes more difficult.
Because while I was thinking about the people who had misunderstood me, another thought began pressing against my heart.
How many times have I misunderstood someone else?
How many times have I reacted too quickly?
How many times have I assumed I knew another person's intentions?
How many times have I allowed frustration to speak before love had an opportunity to listen?
It is easy to recognize injustice when we are the ones receiving it.
It is harder to recognize the same tendency when it lives inside us.
And this is why the Gospel does not allow me to turn this article into a monument to my own innocence.
I am not the hero of this story.
Jesus is.
I am another imperfect person standing in need of the mercy of God.
And when I look at Christ, I see something far greater than a perfect example of how to respond to criticism.
I see the sinless Savior who endured false accusations, unjust condemnation, humiliation, and crucifixion to redeem sinners.
In Mark 14:55–59, the chief priests and the council sought testimony against Jesus, and false witnesses came forward.
Their testimonies did not agree.
Think about that.
The only truly innocent Man who ever lived stood before people determined to condemn Him.
And the evidence presented against Him was unreliable.
Jesus did not deserve what was happening.
Yet He willingly continued toward the cross, fulfilling the Father's redemptive purpose.
Isaiah 53:7 had described the suffering servant as one who, though oppressed and afflicted, did not open His mouth in protest.
That prophecy finds its profound fulfillment in Christ's suffering.
But we must be careful here.
Jesus' silence in the face of certain accusations does not mean Christians must never explain themselves, challenge falsehoods, or seek justice.
Jesus Himself sometimes answered His opponents, exposed hypocrisy, and confronted false accusations.
The lesson is not that truth must always remain silent.
The lesson is that faithfulness to God must govern how we respond.
And nowhere is that truth more astonishing than at Calvary.
Luke 23:34 records Jesus saying:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς· οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν τί ποιοῦσιν.
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." — KJV

A textual note matters here: this saying is included in many ancient manuscripts and traditional Bible translations, though it is absent from some early witnesses. That manuscript question deserves honesty rather than concealment.
Nevertheless, the prayer as traditionally received expresses a mercy fully consistent with Christ's teaching and His sacrificial mission.
Imagine the scene.
The nails.
The mockery.
The soldiers.
The religious hostility.
The suffering.
And from the cross comes a prayer for forgiveness.
Not because evil had suddenly become acceptable.
Not because injustice no longer mattered.
But because the heart of Christ reveals a mercy greater than the cruelty of His enemies.
And suddenly my own situation looks different.
I may have been misunderstood.
I may have received unfair criticism.
But I have also been forgiven of sins far greater than the discomfort of being criticized online.
Christ did not die merely to make me feel justified when people mistreat me.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
He rose again so that those who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness and new life.
And if I truly belong to Him, then even my response to unfair treatment must come under His lordship.
That does not mean pretending harsh words do not hurt.
They do.
Sometimes you spend hours studying Scripture, praying over your words, checking the context, and trying to communicate something that will strengthen another person's faith.
You publish it with the hope that someone struggling might encounter the truth of Jesus.
Then a person reads only a fraction of it and attacks your motives.
It can be exhausting.
It can make you wonder whether the effort is worth it.
It can tempt you to stop writing altogether.
But then you remember the person who quietly messaged you because a passage helped them return to prayer.
The believer who was wrestling with shame and discovered that repentance is not the end of hope.
The person who had almost given up but found encouragement to seek Christ again.
The reader who had never understood grace and began asking sincere questions about the Gospel.
And you remember why the work matters.
Not because every article will be perfect.
Not because everyone will approve.
Not because criticism should be ignored.
But because God's Word is worth studying, proclaiming, and discussing faithfully.
Even when the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Even when misunderstandings happen.
Even when correction is necessary.
And perhaps especially when our pride wants to take control.
Because the real danger is not simply that someone might misjudge an article.
The deeper danger is that we might become so committed to winning an argument that we forget the soul of the person on the other side.
That person is not merely a profile picture.
Not merely a username.
Not merely an opponent in a comment section.
That person is someone made in the image of God.
Someone with fears, wounds, convictions, experiences, and a life we may know almost nothing about.
Perhaps they have been deceived by false teaching before and now react defensively whenever something sounds unfamiliar.
Perhaps they are genuinely concerned about biblical truth.
Perhaps they are struggling with pride.
Perhaps they misunderstood my words.
Perhaps I communicated poorly.
Sometimes more than one of those things can be true.
And love does not require me to pretend every accusation is justified.
It requires me to remember that even those who criticize me are people whom God calls me to treat with dignity.
Second Timothy 2:24–25 reminds us that the servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome but should be gentle, patient, and able to teach, correcting opponents with meekness.
That instruction does not eliminate doctrinal correction.
It tells us what kind of spirit should accompany it.
Truth without love can become a weapon of pride.
Love without truth can become permission for error.
But biblical faithfulness calls us to speak truth in love, as Ephesians 4:15 teaches.
Both matter.
And I want Gospel Warrior to remain a place where both are taken seriously.
Not a place where every disagreement is treated as persecution.
Not a place where biblical correction is dismissed as hatred.
Not a place where people are pressured to agree with everything I write.
But a place where Scripture is examined carefully, questions are welcomed, repentance is taken seriously, and Jesus Christ remains greater than the person holding the pen.
Because I do not want to build a community that merely defends me.
I want to help build a community that follows Christ.
There is a difference.
A community built around a personality becomes fragile whenever that personality is questioned.
A community grounded in God's Word can grow through honest examination, correction, humility, and love.
And if something I publish needs correction, I want to have the courage to acknowledge it.
Not quietly bury it.
Not attack the person who noticed it.
Not protect my image at the expense of the truth.
Because the Gospel I proclaim calls me to repentance too.
The Greek word μετάνοια, metanoia, is commonly translated as repentance.
It carries the sense of a change of mind or understanding, and in the New Testament's call to repentance it involves turning from sin toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone caught us.
It is responding to God's truth with a heart willing to turn.
And that includes how we speak to one another.
It includes how we read.
How we judge.
How we correct.
How we apologize.
How we forgive.
How we handle being misunderstood.
How we handle discovering that we ourselves were wrong.
Sometimes the most powerful Christian witness in a heated conversation is not the longest response.
Sometimes it is the humility to say:
"I misunderstood you. I am sorry."
Or:
"You were right to question that. Let me correct it."
Or:
"I still disagree, but I should not have spoken to you that way."
Those words may never become viral.
But they can reflect the transforming work of the Holy Spirit more clearly than a thousand angry comments.
And I wonder how different our online Christian communities would become if we practiced them more often.
Imagine believers who actually read before responding.
Imagine disagreements where both sides opened Scripture instead of immediately questioning each other's salvation.
Imagine people who could identify false teaching without humiliating those who had been deceived.
Imagine Christian writers who valued correction more than applause.
Imagine readers who cared more about truth than the satisfaction of winning an argument.
Imagine a community where someone could confess, "I was wrong," without being treated as disposable.
That would not be a community without conviction.
It would be a community where conviction had learned to kneel before Christ.
And that is the kind of discipleship I want us to pursue.
So let me say something that may surprise those who expected me to respond to my critics with anger.
To the people who attacked me without reading the whole article, I do not want you to become my enemies.
I want us to seek the truth.
I want us to open the Bible.
I want us to examine what was actually written.
And where we disagree, I want us to disagree in a manner worthy of the Gospel.
If I am wrong, may God give me humility to receive correction.
If you misunderstood me, I hope you will be willing to reconsider.
And if we have both allowed pride to enter the conversation, may God have mercy on both of us.
Because neither of us stands above the cross.
At Calvary, every illusion of self-righteousness must eventually surrender.
The writer.
The critic.
The preacher.
The reader.
The person who has been wounded.
The person who has caused the wound.
We all need the same Savior.
Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Romans 5:8 reveals God's love in Christ dying for us while we were still sinners.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds believers that salvation is by grace through faith, not something we earn through our works.
That means I cannot earn God's favor by publishing Christian articles.
And you cannot earn His favor by correcting them.
Neither of us is saved by winning a theological debate.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us to live differently.
That brings me to something personal.
I want to continue writing.
I want to continue studying Scripture and making biblical resources available.

I want to reach people who are spiritually exhausted, people struggling with sin, people questioning their faith, people who have been wounded by religious hypocrisy, and people who have never truly understood the Gospel.
I want the person who feels too ashamed to enter a church to encounter the truth that Christ receives repentant sinners.
I want the believer who has grown spiritually cold to be reminded that returning to Jesus is more important than maintaining a religious appearance.
I want the Christian who has become angry and combative to rediscover the gentleness and holiness of the Savior.
And I want people who disagree with me to know that sincere questions are not unwelcome.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to make my name great.
But to point people to the name above every name.
Jesus Christ.

And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, encouraged you to return to Scripture, helped you understand the Gospel, or reminded you that God's grace is still calling you to repentance, I want to invite you to become part of what we are building.
Not through guilt.
Not through the suggestion that God loves paying supporters more.
It isn't.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of generosity, partnership, and love.
In Philippians 4:15–18, Paul speaks appreciatively of believers who shared with him in the work of ministry through their financial gifts.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, he teaches that giving should come from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
These passages provide a biblical foundation for voluntary generosity.
Your responsibilities to your local church, your family, and those in need remain important.
It can help us keep producing Scripture-centered articles, developing discipleship materials, expanding the resources we share, and reaching more people with the message of Christ.
And I want to be clear.
You are not buying God's blessing. You are choosing to help make Gospel-centered resources available to others.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
Your worth before God is not measured by your financial contribution.
Your place in the family of Christ is not purchased through a monthly payment.
Jesus Christ has already accomplished what no amount of money could ever accomplish through His death and resurrection.
The invitation to support is an invitation to partnership, not a condition of belonging.
And there is another way you can help that costs nothing.
Not merely because I want more people to read my words.
Someone may be carrying the pain of being falsely accused.
Someone may be using biblical truth as an excuse for cruelty.
Someone may need the courage to apologize.
Someone may need to forgive.
And someone may be one honest conversation away from reconsidering what they believe about Jesus Christ.
A simple share can place a message before someone who might never have searched for it.
If a particular person comes to mind, consider tagging them with kindness, not as a public rebuke or an attempt to embarrass them, but as an invitation to reflect together.
Not because every sentence I have written deserves to be remembered.
But because the next time you feel the urge to respond angrily to something you have not fully understood, James 1:19 and Proverbs 18:13 may be exactly what your heart needs.
Return to those passages.
Let Scripture correct your instincts.
Let it correct mine too.
I also want to hear from you.
Not just the people who agree with me.
I want to hear from those who have been misunderstood, those who have misunderstood others, and those who have learned painful lessons about speaking too quickly.
Have you ever been judged before someone understood your side of the story? Or have you ever had to admit that you judged someone too quickly?
You do not need to share private details or identify the people involved.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another believer that they are not alone in their struggle.
Your story may encourage someone who is still wrestling with theirs.
Not because following a page makes anyone a disciple of Christ.
But because regular exposure to sound biblical teaching, encouragement, honest questions, and Scripture-centered reflection can become one helpful part of a much larger journey of discipleship.
Because we want people to grow in God's Word, not merely support a platform.
I want to return to the very thing that made me write this article.
The accusations.
The misunderstanding.
The temptation to defend myself.
Because after everything I have said, the most important question is no longer whether everyone will finally understand me.
Some will.
Some will not.
Some may still disagree after reading every word.
And some may identify genuine mistakes that I need to correct.
That is part of being human.
That is part of speaking publicly.
And it is part of remaining accountable to the Word of God.
But my calling is not to make everyone approve of me.
My calling is to be faithful to Christ.
To speak truthfully.
To remain teachable.
To refuse needless cruelty.
To correct error without despising people.
To receive correction without surrendering to pride.
To forgive without pretending wrongdoing is harmless.
And to remember that the person who opposes me today is not beyond the reach of the same grace that rescued me.
Perhaps that is what I needed to learn through all of this.
Not that criticism should stop.
Not that everyone should agree.
But that the Gospel must shape my heart even when my heart is hurting.
Because there is a terrible possibility that every Christian writer, teacher, reader, and commentator must confront.
We can become so consumed with defending the truth that we forget to obey it.
We can become so determined to expose another person's mistakes that we refuse to examine our own.
We can become so skilled at explaining grace that we forget to extend it.
And if that happens, we may win an argument while losing an opportunity to reflect the character of Christ.
I do not want that.
I do not want it for myself.
I do not want it for the people who criticize me.
I want something better.
I want us to become people who love Scripture enough to read it carefully.
People who love truth enough to welcome correction.
People who love others enough to listen.
People who love Jesus enough to repent.
And people who understand that grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is the undeserved favor of God that saves sinners and teaches those who belong to Christ to turn from ungodliness and pursue lives that honor Him, as Titus 2:11–14 teaches.
So if you came here expecting me to attack the people who attacked me, I hope you have discovered something different.
I am not asking you to choose my side.
I am asking all of us to examine our hearts before God.
And if you were one of the people who judged my writing without reading it fully, I invite you to begin again.
Read.
Ask.
Examine.
Disagree where Scripture gives you reason to disagree.
Correct me where correction is warranted.
But please do not let an assumption become a verdict before the evidence has been heard.
And I will ask God to help me extend the same fairness to you.
Because the cross leaves no room for the illusion that I am always right.
It leaves room for confession.
For mercy.
For repentance.
For forgiveness.
For transformation.
For the person who has been misunderstood.
And for the person who misunderstood them.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
The final word over a repentant sinner does not have to be the worst thing they have said, believed, or done.
In Christ, there is forgiveness.
In Christ, there is redemption.
In Christ, there is hope for a genuinely changed life.

And if the Lord can take sinners who were once enemies of God and reconcile them to Himself through the death of His Son, as Romans 5:10 teaches, then surely we can ask Him to help us approach one another with greater humility.
The world already has enough people shouting past each other.
May the church become a place where truth is loved, Scripture is honored, sin is confronted, and grace is neither forgotten nor abused.
May our words point beyond our wounded pride.
May our corrections be faithful.
May our apologies be sincere.
May our forgiveness reflect the mercy we have received.
And may Jesus Christ be glorified whether people praise us, question us, correct us, or misunderstand us.
Because this story was never meant to end with me being vindicated.
It was meant to lead us back to the Savior who alone can make sinners righteous before God.

Perhaps the deepest tragedy is not being misunderstood by someone who never finished reading our words, but becoming so consumed with defending ourselves that we stop listening to the voice of Christ calling us to become more like Him.
